claims.text: Boron microalloying in HEA coatings leads to the formation of fine-scale boride precipitates.
Boron microalloying modifies grain-boundary chemistry in HEA coatings.
Boride formation increases the hardness of HEA coatings.
The increased hardness produced by boride formation reduces mechanical wear.
Boron promotes formation of a more stable protective passive film at critical microstructural locations.
A more stable protective passive film mitigates corrosion.
The wear- and corrosion-resistance mechanisms act synergistically to reduce overall material degradation.
HEA coatings without boron exhibit a typical multiphase microstructure and characteristic grain boundaries.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, boron-microalloyed HEA coatings will have a lower wear rate than matched boron-free coatings.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, boron-microalloyed HEA coatings will have a lower corrosion rate than matched boron-free coatings.
Combined degradation of boron-microalloyed HEA coatings will be lower than the sum of their separately measured wear and corrosion contributions.
An optimized boron concentration forms beneficial boride phases and permits improved tribocorrosion resistance.
Excess boron can produce brittle or overly segregated phases.
Brittle or overly segregated phases formed at excessive boron levels can eliminate the predicted improvement in resistance.
The magnitude of degradation-rate reduction varies with boron concentration and processing conditions.
